checksum.title: What is a checksum?
checksum.p1: A checksum is a short string of letters and numbers calculated from the contents of a file, like a fingerprint. Change a single bit in the file and the checksum changes completely. Identical files always produce identical checksums.
checksum.p2: Publishers list a checksum next to their download. You calculate it for the file you received and compare. If the two match, the file is exactly what the publisher released. If they don’t, the download is broken or has been altered.
steps: Copy the checksum from the official download page, or save their checksum file (.sha256, .md5, .txt, …).
Drop your downloaded file here and paste the value, or upload the checksum file.
A match means the file is identical. No match means download it again from the official source.
trust: SHA-256 is today’s standard and our recommendation. SHA-512, SHA-3 and BLAKE3 are equally strong.
SHA-1 and MD5 still detect accidental damage but can be forged on purpose, so don’t rely on them for security.
CRC32, CRC32C, Adler-32 and Fletcher are small error-detection codes used in archives and networking. They are not secure.
checksum.note: A checksum shows that two files are the same, not that the file is safe. It is only as trustworthy as the place you copied it from.

faq.a: No. Checksums are calculated in your browser, so your file never leaves your device.

faq.q: How large a file can I check?
faq.a: Almost any size, including multi-gigabyte files. The file is read in 8 MB pieces, so larger files just take longer. Keep the tab open until the progress bar finishes.

faq.q: Do capital letters and spaces matter?
faq.a: No, both are ignored. Put each checksum on its own line. You can also paste or upload a whole checksum file, including lines like hash *filename or MD5 (filename) = hash. Lines starting with # are skipped.

faq.q: Why are there so many checksum types?
faq.a: Download sites use different ones, so SumVerify checks the common types automatically. If none match, you can check the other types too.

faq.q: My checksum doesn’t match. What now?
faq.a: Make sure you copied the whole value and that it belongs to this exact file and version. Then download the file again from the official source. If it still doesn’t match, don’t open it.

faq.q: Does a match mean the file is safe?
faq.a: No. A match only proves the file is identical to the one the checksum was made from. Always get both from a trusted source.
A coming-soon feature that checks whether your file’s checksum matches a known file in our own database. Only the checksum is sent, never the file.

faq.q: Is SumVerify free and open source?
faq.a: Yes, free forever and MIT-licensed. Report bugs or contribute on {githubLink}.

about.intro: SumVerify is a free checksum calculator and file verifier that runs entirely in your browser. Drop a file, paste the hash published by the download page, and see at once whether the two match.

ui.matchMany: Match. The {types} hashes match{note}. This file is identical to the original.

ui.riskWeak: Security warning: {types} only detects accidental errors and gives no protection against tampering, so the security risk is high. Don’t rely on this match to trust the file: compare a SHA-256 hash from the official site instead.
ui.comparing: Comparing… no match yet, still calculating. Results appear one hash type at a time.

ui.noMatchCommon: No match with the common hash types. If your hash uses a different format, check the other types too. {button}

ui.noMatchOne: The hash you provided doesn’t match this file in any of the {total} hash types.
ui.noMatchMany: None of the {count} hashes you provided matches this file in any of the {total} hash types.

secure.strong: Yes. {name} is considered strong: no practical way to forge a matching file is known, so it is a good choice for checking downloads.
secure.medium: For spotting a broken or incomplete download, yes. But {name} is an older type, and researchers have shown ways to build two different files with the same {name}. If the site also offers {successor}, compare that one too.
secure.weak: Not for security. {name} is designed to catch accidental errors, not tampering, and a changed file can be made to match it on purpose. Treat a match as a basic sanity check and compare {successor} when you can.

faq.a: A {name} checksum is {bits} bits long, which is written as {hexLen} characters using the digits 0–9 and the letters a–f. Capital letters and spaces don’t matter.

faq.q: Can I compare a different hash type with {name}?
faq.a: No. A {name} value only matches another {name} value, so use the type named on the download page. The length ({hexLen} characters) is a hint, but several types share it. If you’re unsure, press “Check other hash types” above.

hashes.sha256: SHA-256 is the most widely used checksum today. Linux downloads, apps, firmware and developer tools usually publish a SHA-256 value, and its 64-character code is the one to trust first.
hashes.md5: MD5 is a classic 32-character checksum. Many websites, backups and old programs still list it because it is quick to calculate. It catches broken downloads well, but it was not built to stop tampering.
hashes.sha1: SHA-1 was the standard for years and still appears next to older downloads and inside Git. It is fine for spotting a broken download, but newer files should use SHA-256.
hashes.sha512: SHA-512 is SHA-256’s bigger sibling. It produces a longer 128-character code and is common on Linux distributions, security tools and servers. It is just as safe, only more thorough.
hashes.crc32: CRC32 is a quick 8-character code made to catch accidental errors. ZIP and PNG files, game mods and .sfv lists on archive sites use it to confirm that nothing got corrupted.
hashes.blake2b: BLAKE2b is a fast, modern checksum with a 128-character code. It is popular in security software and developer tools, and it is quicker than SHA-512 on most computers.
hashes.blake3: BLAKE3 is one of the newest and fastest checksums, with a 64-character code. It handles huge files quickly and is gaining ground in modern developer tools and backups.
hashes.crc32c: CRC32C is a faster cousin of CRC32 with an 8-character code. Storage systems, databases and network protocols use it to catch damaged data, often with help from your processor.
hashes.sha384: SHA-384 is a shortened form of SHA-512 with a 96-character code. You will meet it in secure connections and some signed packages, where a strong but slightly shorter result is wanted.
hashes.sha3-256: SHA3-256 is the most common SHA-3 variant, with a 64-character code. It is built differently from SHA-256, which is why some projects publish it as a second opinion.
hashes.sha224: SHA-224 is a trimmed-down version of SHA-256 that gives a 56-character code. It is rarer on download pages but still shows up in older systems and some embedded devices.
hashes.sha3-512: SHA3-512 is the longest standard SHA-3 result, a 128-character code. It is used where maximum strength is wanted and is rarer on everyday download pages.
hashes.blake2s: BLAKE2s is the lighter version of BLAKE2, made for smaller devices. Its 64-character code is strong, and you will find it in some apps and tools that value speed.
hashes.sha3-384: SHA3-384 is a mid-size SHA-3 option with a 96-character code. It turns up in high-security software and standards that ask for extra strength.
hashes.sha3-224: SHA3-224 comes from SHA-3, the newest official family. Built differently from SHA-2, it gives a 56-character code and acts as an independent backup if SHA-2 ever weakens.
hashes.md4: MD4 is a very old 32-character checksum from 1990. You will rarely see it today, mostly with legacy systems and file-sharing links such as eDonkey (ed2k). Use it only to match an old value.
hashes.adler32: Adler-32 is a very simple 8-character check built into the zlib and PNG formats. It runs fast but is easy to fool, so it is only for catching accidental corruption.
hashes.crc16: CRC16 is a tiny 4-character code for catching errors. It lives mostly in hardware, industrial gear, serial links and embedded devices, where small size matters more than strength.
hashes.fletcher32: Fletcher-32 is the 8-character version of Fletcher’s check. It is used in some embedded and storage software, and is best seen as a quick error check, not protection.
hashes.fletcher16: Fletcher-16 is a light 4-character check from the 1980s. It is still found in older network and embedded software, where speed and tiny size mattered most.
hashes.crc8: CRC8 is the smallest of the family, just 2 characters. It guards very short messages in sensors, batteries and small chips, so a match here proves very little on its own.
